Britannica entry (CAPPARIS):
<britannica>
CAPPARIS, in botany : A genus of the mono-gynia order, belonging to the polyandria clafs of plants; and in the natural method ranking under the 25th order, Putaminae. The calyx is tetraphyllous and cori-aceous; there petals are four; the flamina are long; the fruit is a berry, carnous, unilocular, and pedunca-lated, or furnished with a foot-falk. There are fewer species. The fpinofa, or common caper, is a low shrub, generally growing out of the joints of old walls, the fifures of rocks, and a-mongit rubbifh, in molt of the warm parts of Europe: it hath woody flalks, which fend out many lateral flen-der branches: under each of thefe are placed two short crooked fpines, between which and the branches come out the foottitalks of the leaves, which are fingle, flort, and fulltain a round fnooth entire leaf. At the inter-mediate joints, between the branches, come out the flowers on long foottitalks; before thefe expand, the bud with the empalement is gathered for pickling. Thofe which are left expand in form of a fingle role, having five large white petals, which are roundifh and concave; in the middle are placed a great number of long flamina, furrounding a flyle which rifes above them, and crowned with an oval germen, which afterwards becomes a capfulle filled with kidney-shaped feeds. Culture. This plant is very differently preserved in Britain: it delights to grow in crevices of rocks, old walls, c. and always thrives beft in an horizontal po-flure; fo that, when planted either in pots or in the full ground, they felddom thrive, though they may be kept alive for fome years. They are propagated by feeds in the warm parts of Europe, but very felddom in Britain. Ufer. The buds, pickled with vinegar, c. are brought to Britain annually from Italy and the Mediterranean. They are fuppofed to excite appetite and afflit digestion; and to be particularly useful as deter- gents and aperients in obtitractions of the liver and spleen.
</britannica>

[1] Capparis is a genus of flowering plants in the family Capparaceae. It includes about 140 species of shrubs or lianas which are collectively known as caper shrubs or caperbushes. Capparis species occur over a wide range of habitat in the subtropical and tropical regions of Africa, Eurasia, Australasia, and the Pacific. The genus was included in the family Brassicaceae in the unrevised APG II system. The leaves are simple, entire, and rarely reduced. Flowers are bisexual, bracteates, axillary or supra-axillary, solitary or in rows, in racemes or umbels. Sepals and petals are 4 in number and are free. Stamens are many, ovary on a gynophore, one-celled. Fruit is a berry, globose or ellipsoid. Caperbushes are mainly used by humans for their fruit, which are rich in micronutrients. C. spinosa, simply known as caper, yields fruit and more importantly flower buds, which are widely used pickled as a vegetable condiment. The flower bud has been used since antiquity, and many classical authors indicate that the berry or small white blossom was commonly used as an aphrodisiac and a condiment.
